sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: BI 1701963 is a small-molecule son of sevenless 1 (SOS1) inhibitor that selectively binds to SOS1, blocking the protein–protein interaction of SOS1 with guanosine diphosphate-bound rat sarcoma virus (RAS) proteins [Kirsten RAS (KRAS), Harvey RAS, and neuroblastoma RAS], thereby inhibiting the growth of RAS-dependent cancer cells.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Three phase I dose-escalation studies evaluated BI 1701963 as monotherapy (starting dose of 50 mg) or in combination with trametinib (starting dose of 100 mg/1 mg) in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors (NCT04111458, USA and Europe; NCT04835714, Japan; and NCT04627142, China). Primary endpoints were maximum tolerated dose (MTD) based on dose-limiting toxicities (DLT; part A NCT04111458) and the number of patients with DLT in the MTD evaluation period (part A NCT04111458 and NCT04835714) or the on-treatment period (Part B NCT04835714).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Ninety-four patients were treated: 75 with monotherapy (50–800 mg) and 19 in combination (100 mg/1 mg; 100 mg/1.5 mg; and 200 mg/1 mg). Six monotherapy patients (8%) and six combination patients (31.6%) experienced DLT in the MTD evaluation period. All patients experienced adverse events; of note, three monotherapy patients had interstitial lung disease during the first treatment cycle, leading to death, which was considered drug-related by the investigator. In the monotherapy group, one patient (1.8%) experienced a partial response, and 12 patients (21.8%) had stable disease. In the combination group, four patients (33.3%) had stable disease, carrying different KRAS alleles.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: BI 1701963 treatment demonstrated limited efficacy as monotherapy. MTD was determined to be 800-mg monotherapy (NCT04111458) and 100 mg/1 mg in combination with trametinib (NCT04111458).

boxed-text.p: Currently, there are no approved targeted therapies for patients with tumors with Kirsten RAS (KRAS) mutations (except KRASG12C). BI 1701963 is a small-molecule son of sevenless 1 (SOS1) inhibitor that selectively binds to SOS1, blocking the protein–protein interaction of SOS1 with guanosine diphosphate-bound rat sarcoma virus (RAS) proteins (KRAS, Harvey RAS, and neuroblastoma RAS), thus inhibiting the growth of RAS-dependent cancer cells. We report the findings from three phase I dose-escalation studies evaluating BI 1701963 as monotherapy and in combination with trametinib in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors [NCT04111458, USA and Europe (monotherapy and combination); NCT04835714, Japan; and NCT04627142, China (monotherapy only)]. BI 1701963 was generally manageable as monotherapy; limited efficacy was observed. The maximum tolerated dose was determined to be 800 mg for monotherapy and 100 mg/1 mg in combination with trametinib (NCT04111458). NCT04835714 and NCT04627142 were discontinued following a risk–benefit analysis. These data will inform future research into therapies for KRAS mutation-positive cancers.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Rat sarcoma virus (RAS) proteins, including Kirsten RAS (KRAS), Harvey RAS (HRAS), and neuroblastoma RAS (NRAS), are small membrane-bound guanosine triphosphatases that function as molecular switches. Upon binding to guanosine triphosphate (GTP), RAS proteins cycle to the activated “on” state and activate several downstream pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, which controls a range of cellular processes, such as proliferation, survival, and migration (1–4). Mutations in RAS genes lead to the overactivation of RAS proteins, upregulating MAPK signaling and driving the growth of RAS mutation-positive tumors (1, 4).

Approximately one in seven of all human cancers harbor KRAS alterations, making KRAS one of the top oncogenic drivers (1, 5, 6). KRAS mutations and amplification of wild-type KRAS are found predominantly in pancreatic cancer (∼90% of cases), colorectal cancer (∼45% of cases), and non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; ∼35% of cases; refs. 1, 2, 6).

Targeting KRAS and other RAS proteins in cancer has been a central therapeutic goal for the past 4 decades (1). Two KRASG12C inhibitors, sotorasib and adagrasib, have received accelerated U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval and conditional European Medicines Agency approval for the treatment of second-line KRASG12C mutation-positive NSCLC, based on phase II studies CodeBreaK 100 and KRYSTAL-1 [objective response (OR) rates of 37.1% and 42.9%, respectively; refs. 7, 8]. KRAS inhibitors combined with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-targeting mAb have shown promise, with adagrasib plus cetuximab and sotorasib plus panitumumab receiving FDA approval in adult patients with KRASG12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic colorectal cancer in recent years (9–11). Additional KRASG12C inhibitors in clinical development include divarasib (GDC-6036), garsorasib (D-1553), and olomorasib (LY3537982; refs. 12–14). Glecirasib (JAB-21822) has received orphan drug designation in the U.S. (15) and breakthrough therapy designation in China for KRASG12C-mutated pancreatic cancer (16). Fulzerasib has been approved in China for use in later-line KRASG12C-mutated NSCLC (17). However, these mutant-selective inhibitors specifically target tumors with the KRASG12C mutation, which are present in only ∼13.6% of tumors (1).

More than 85% of all KRAS-mutated cancers still lack effective therapies; therefore, there is an unmet need for new therapy options that target a broad range of KRAS mutations, including mutant KRASG12C, KRASG12D, KRASG12V, KRASG13D, KRASG12R, and KRASG12A (1).

Guanine nucleotide exchange factor son of sevenless 1 (SOS1) is the “on-switch” for RAS signaling, acting to catalyze the exchange of RAS-GDP for RAS-GTP. Therefore, targeting SOS1 presents an opportunity to inhibit all forms of RAS signaling. BI 1701963 is a small-molecule inhibitor that selectively binds to SOS1, blocking the protein–protein interaction with guanosine diphosphate–bound RAS (including KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS). By preventing this interaction, BI 1701963 reduces the amount of activated GTP-bound RAS. In KRAS-mutant tumors, BI 1701963 can reduce the levels of GTP-bound KRAS, reducing MAPK signaling and resulting in inhibited growth of KRAS-dependent cancer cells (1).

MAPK pathway components downstream of RAS, such as MEK, are other candidates for targeted therapy. The effectiveness of MEK inhibitors is limited by the development of resistance, thought to derive from the persistence of MAPK signaling supported by feedback-driven pathway rebound (18, 19). Preclinical data have demonstrated that combining a MEK inhibitor (e.g., trametinib) with a SOS1 inhibitor leads to enhanced inhibition of the MAPK signaling pathway (20). Based on these data, it was hypothesized that the combination of BI 1701963 with a MEK inhibitor may lead to improved efficacy versus BI 1701963 monotherapy in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors.

Here, we report pooled safety, preliminary efficacy, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic data from three phase I studies of BI 1701963 alone or in combination with trametinib in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors.

sec.title: Study designs
sec.p: We conducted three phase I, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion studies of BI 1701963 as monotherapy or in combination with trametinib in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Study design: studies NCT04111458, NCT04835714, and NCT04627142.

sec.p: NCT04111458 (U.S. and Europe) was a first-in-human, multicenter study that assessed BI 1701963 as monotherapy and in combination with trametinib in patients with previously treated, relapsed/refractory, KRAS mutation-positive advanced or metastatic solid tumors. The study had two arms (monotherapy and in combination with trametinib) and two parts [dose escalation (part A) and confirmation (part B)]. Primary objectives were to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or recommended phase II dose (RP2D) of BI 1701963 as monotherapy and in combination with trametinib, based on dose-limiting toxicities (DLT). Secondary objectives were to evaluate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary efficacy.

NCT04835714 was designed to assess BI 1701963 as monotherapy in Japanese patients with previously treated, relapsed/refractory, KRAS mutation-positive advanced/metastatic solid tumors. The primary objectives were to determine the MTD and/or RP2D of BI 1701963. The secondary objective was to characterize the pharmacokinetics.

NCT04627142 was conducted in China and was designed to assess BI 1701963 in patients with previously treated, relapsed/refractory, KRAS mutation-positive unresectable locally advanced or metastatic colorectal cancer. The study aimed to evaluate the safety and tolerability, to characterize the pharmacokinetics, and to explore preliminary efficacy signals of BI 1701963 monotherapy.

The studies were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines and were approved by the local institutional review boards. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Eligible patients were aged ≥ 18 years (or over the legal age of consent as required by local legislation), had an identified KRAS activation mutation in tumor tissue before screening, had archived tumor tissue (NCT04111458 and NCT04835714), were willing to undergo pre- and on-treatment tumor biopsies (studies NCT04111458 and NCT04835714; patients in study NCT04835714 could be recruited without biopsy if agreed upon between the sponsor and investigator and if biopsy was clinically contraindicated), had at least one target lesion that could be measured per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1), had documented disease progression despite appropriate prior standard therapies, or had no standard therapy options available (monotherapy arm of study NCT04111458 and study NCT04835714), with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, adequate organ function, and had fully recovered from any previous therapy-related toxicity of grade ≥1.
Patients in study NCT04627142 were additionally required to have received at least first-line chemotherapy.

Key exclusion criteria included previous treatment with KRAS-, MAPK-, or SOS1-targeting agents; the presence of uncontrolled or symptomatic brain metastases; previous anticancer chemotherapy within 3 weeks; anticancer hormonal treatment within 2 weeks; and anticancer immunotherapy within 2 weeks (studies NCT04111458 and NCT04627142) or 3 weeks (study NCT04835714) before the first administration of study drugs.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: In study NCT04111458, dose tiers in the monotherapy part A started at BI 1701963 50 mg once daily administered orally (Fig. 1). Based on preclinical data, the human-predicted efficacious dose to achieve a reduction of tumor growth was 420 mg. Dose escalation was determined by the Safety Monitoring Committee (SMC), guided by a Bayesian logistic regression model (BLRM) with overdose control, until the MTD or a maximum dose of 2,000 mg was reached. Once the 200-mg monotherapy dose level was confirmed as safe (50% of the human therapeutic dose based on a pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic model in NMRI nude mice), dose escalation for BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib was initiated, with a starting dose of BI 1701963 100 mg and trametinib 1 mg once daily given orally. Dose escalation was determined by the SMC until the MTD of the combination, the highest dose of BI 1701963 tested in the monotherapy arm, was reached, or the maximum dose of trametinib, 2 mg, was reached.

In NCT04835714, BI 1701963 dose tiers started at 400 mg once daily orally (Fig. 1). Escalation steps were guided by a BLRM with overdose control and continued until the MTD, a maximum of 2,000 mg, or the MTD of NCT04111458 was reached.

In NCT04627142, the starting dosage for BI 1701963 monotherapy was 400 mg once daily orally (Fig. 1). Dose escalation steps were determined by the SMC, guided by a BLRM model with overdose control, until the MTD or the highest dose of BI 1701963 was confirmed safe in NCT04111458.

A starting dose of BI 1701963 at 400 mg was selected for NCT04835714 and NCT04627142 because 400 mg was confirmed as a safe dose in the NCT04111458 monotherapy dose-escalation trial, completed by the time of initiation of the two subsequent trials.
In all studies, patients continued treatment until progressive disease, undue drug toxicity, or withdrawal of consent.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessment
sec.p: Primary and secondary endpoints for each study are summarized in Supplementary Table S1.
For all studies, tumor response was evaluated according to RECIST v1.1 every 8 weeks until progressive disease, initiation of subsequent anticancer therapy, death, or the end of the trial.
Adverse events (AE) were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.

In NCT04111458, fresh tumor biopsies were collected at screening and day 16 (cycle 1) for pharmacodynamic and biomarker analyses. Inhibition of the MAPK pathway by SOS1 inhibitors in preclinical models showed a dose-dependent decrease in pERK and Ki-67 proliferative index. Based on these results, paired clinical biopsies were collected for immunohistochemical (IHC) assessment of the Ki-67 proliferation index and pERK (a member of the RAS–MAPK signaling cascade) H-score across dose groups.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Dose escalation was guided by a BLRM with overdose control that was fitted to binary toxicity outcomes using a hierarchical modeling approach. The estimates of the model parameters were updated as data were accumulated using the BLRM. At the end of the dose escalation, the toxicity probability at each dose level was calculated to determine an estimate of the MTD.

The MTD was defined as the highest dose with a ≤ 25% risk of the true DLT rate being equal to or above 33% during the MTD evaluation period [first treatment cycle (28 days)]. The RP2D was determined by the SMC, defined as any dose that fulfilled the escalation with overdose control criterion. The SMC could decide to declare a dose as the RP2D without determining the MTD, through consideration of all available data, including that from preceding trials.

sec.title: Patients and treatment
sec.p: Start and end dates for the studies were as follows: NCT04111458: November 4, 2019, to November 23, 2021 (date of the interim cutoff for part A); NCT04835714: April 30, 2021, to January 18, 2022; and NCT04627142: December 23, 2020, to January 18, 2022.

In total, 94 patients with KRAS-mutated advanced or metastatic solid tumors had been treated at the data cutoff date (August 5, 2023, for patients receiving BI 1701963 monotherapy and December 23, 2021, for patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib; Fig. 2). Seventy-five patients received BI 1701963 monotherapy (NCT04111458, n = 52; NCT04835714, n = 8; and NCT04627142, n = 15), and 19 patients received BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib (NCT04111458). Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The most common tumor types were colorectal cancer (60% and 47.4%), pancreatic cancer (17.3% and 31.6%), and NSCLC (10.7% and 15.8%) in the monotherapy and combination arms, respectively. Most patients had received ≥ 2 lines of treatment in both the monotherapy (71%) and combination arms (89.5%). The most common KRAS mutation allele was G12D in both arms (monotherapy, 32%; combination therapy, 42.1%). The representativeness of the study population to the real-world population is described in Supplementary Table S2.

caption.p: Summary of baseline characteristics in patients treated with BI 1701963 monotherapy and in combination with trametinib.

sec.p: The 75 patients treated with BI 1701963 monotherapy received doses between 50 and 800 mg (Fig. 2), with a median time on treatment of 42 days (range, 5–175 days). All patients receiving BI 1701963 monotherapy had discontinued treatment at the data cutoff.

The 19 patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib in NCT04111458 received doses of 100 mg/1 mg (n = 5; Fig. 2), 100 mg/1.5 mg (n = 5), or 200 mg/1 mg (n = 9); the median time on treatment was 56 days (range, 1–319 days). At the data cutoff, one patient with KRASG12D-mutated cancer was still on treatment [BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib in study NCT04111458; 50 mg/0.5 mg (dose reduced due to AE, according to protocol); treatment duration at the data cutoff: > 2 years].

sec.title: MTD
sec.p: Of the 75 patients treated with BI 1701963 monotherapy, six (8%) had DLT during the first treatment cycle: three patients with interstitial lung disease [ILD; grade 3 (becoming grade 5 by day 44) and grade 5 at 800 mg, n = 2, NCT04627142; grade 5 at 600 mg, n = 1, NCT04835714], one patient with grade 3 dilated cardiomyopathy (800 mg; NCT04111458), one patient with grade 4 decreased platelet count (800 mg; NCT04111458), and one patient with grade 3 pneumonia (600 mg; NCT04835714).
In NCT04111458, the MTD of BI 1701963 monotherapy was determined to be 800 mg, based on two DLT observed in two of nine patients (22.2%) treated at this dosage.

Of the 19 patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib in NCT04111458, six (31.6%) had DLT in the first treatment cycle: one patient with grade 3 hypertension (100 mg/1 mg), one patient with grade 3 rash (100 mg/1.5 mg), one patient with grade 3 increased alanine aminotransferase (100 mg/1.5 mg), one patient with grade 4 hypertension (200 mg/1 mg), one patient with grade 3 increased transaminases (200 mg/1 mg), and one patient with grade 2 retinopathy (200 mg/1 mg). It was concluded that the MTD of BI 1701963 plus trametinib had been reached at the first dose level investigated (100 mg/1 mg).

sec.title: Safety and tolerability
sec.p: All patients receiving BI 1701963 monotherapy (n = 75) had an AE (Table 2), including four patients (5.3%) with grade 1, 21 patients (28%) with grade 2, 31 patients (41.3%) with grade 3, three patients (4%) with grade 4, and 16 (21.3%) patients with grade 5 any-cause AE, respectively. Sixty patients (80%) had drug-related AE as assessed by the investigator, including 19 patients (25.3%) with grade 3, one patient (1.3%) with grade 4, and three patients (4%) with grade 5 drug-related AE; hypertension and hypocalcemia were the most common grade ≥ 3 drug-related AE (10.7% each). The grade 4 drug-related AE was decreased platelet count (NCT04111458, 800 mg; DLT); grade 5 drug-related AE were all ILD (NCT04835714, 600 mg, n = 1; NCT04627142, 800 mg, n = 2).

caption.p: Summary of adverse events in patients treated with BI 1701963 monotherapy (studies NCT04111458, NCT04835714, and NCT04627142).

sec.p: Seventeen patients (22.7%) discontinued treatment due to an AE. The most common AE leading to treatment discontinuation were ILD and decreased platelet count, both at a frequency of 2.7%. Three patients (4%) had an AE that led to dose reduction [restrictive pulmonary disease (800 mg), decreased platelet count (800 mg), and thrombocytopenia (600 mg)].
Serious AE were reported for 39 patients (52%): most commonly malignant neoplasm progression (10.7%), abdominal pain, ileus, ILD, and pyrexia (4% each).

Sixteen patients (21.3%) had serious AE leading to death, of which three (4%) were assessed as drug-related by the investigator. These three drug-related fatal cases were all interstitial lung disease in Asian patients with colorectal cancer during the first treatment cycle. In the 600-mg cohort (n = 1), treatment duration was 1 day and the KRAS mutational allele was G12A (study NCT04835714). In the 800-mg cohort (n = 2), treatment duration was 14 and 21 days, and KRAS mutational alleles were G12D and other (study NCT04627142). All patients had lung and lymph node metastases; two had liver metastases; and pleural effusion, peritoneal, and other metastases were reported in one patient each. These patients had all received prior chemotherapy, and one patient in study NCT04627142 had received prior radiotherapy (liver lesions). Thirteen (17.3%) fatal cases were considered unrelated to BI 1701963, including malignant neoplasm progression (n = 8), sepsis (n = 2), disease progression (n = 1), large intestine perforation (n = 1), and respiratory failure (n = 1).

All 19 patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib had any-cause AE (Table 3). Three patients (15.8%) had grade 2, 13 patients (68.4%) had grade 3, one patient (5.3%) had grade 4, and two patients (10.5%) had grade 5 any-cause AE, respectively. All patients had drug-related AE (as assessed by the investigator), including 11 patients (57.9%) with grade 3 and one patient (5.3%) with grade 4 drug-related AE. Hypertension was the most frequent grade 3 drug-related AE (15.8%) and the only grade 4 drug-related AE (5.3%).

caption.p: Summary of adverse events in patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib (study NCT04111458).

sec.p: Eight patients (42.1%) discontinued treatment due to an AE, most commonly due to hypertension (n = 2, 10.5%). Dose was reduced due to an AE in five patients (26.3%), most commonly due to rash (n = 2, 10.5%).

Nine patients (47.4%) had serious AE; none of the serious AE were reported for more than one patient. Two of the nine patients had a serious AE leading to death [both considered unrelated to BI 1701963: malignant neoplasm progression, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)].

sec.title: Antitumor activity
sec.p: Fifty-five (73.3%) of the 75 patients treated with BI 1701963 monotherapy had post-baseline tumor assessments (Table 4; Supplementary Table S3). Of these patients, one with a p.G12D KRAS mutation (1.8%; 800 mg, NCT04111458) had a partial response, 12 with either p.G12D, p.G12V, p.G13D, p.G12A, p.G12S, p.G12E, or C.35G>A:P.GLY12ASP mutations [21.8%; NCT04111458, 50 mg (n = 1), 100 mg (n = 3), 400 mg (n = 3), 600 mg (n = 1), and 800 mg (n = 1); NCT04627142, 400 mg (n = 1) and 800 mg (n = 2)] had stable disease, and 38 [69.1%; NCT04111458, 50 mg (n = 2), 100 mg (n = 3), 200 mg (n = 3), 400 mg (n = 8), 600 mg (n = 8), and 800 mg (n = 4); NCT04835714, 400 mg (n = 4) and 600 mg (n = 1); NCT04627142, 400 mg (n = 3) and 800 mg (n = 2)] had disease progression as confirmed best overall response. Overall response and disease control rates were low, despite rapid absorption of BI 1701963 as shown by the median maximum observed plasma concentration (Cmax) being reached 1 to 5 hours after the first dose and dose-dependent exposure area under the plasma concentration time curve (AUC) with moderate to high observed variability (Supplementary Fig. S1). The disease control rate was 23.6%. Response by KRAS mutation type is summarized in Supplementary Table S3.

sec.p: Twelve (63.2%) of the 19 patients treated with BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib in study NCT04111458 had post-baseline measurements (Table 4); of these patients, four (33.3%) had stable disease, and eight (66.7%) had disease progression. One patient exhibited stable disease from baseline until day 278 and remained on treatment for 319 days at the time of data cutoff.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: BI 1701963 was rapidly absorbed; median Cmax was reached 1 to 5 hours after the first dose; thereafter, BI 1701963 concentrations declined in a biphasic manner (Supplementary Fig. S1).

A summary of pharmacokinetic data is presented in Supplementary Table S4. The AUC and Cmax of BI 1701963 increased with increasing doses on days 1 and 15, accumulating by a factor of 2 and 1.5 following repeated doses of 50 to 400 mg in study NCT04111458 and by a factor of 4 to 5 in studies NCT04835714 and NCT04627142, respectively. After administration of 600- and 800-mg doses, on average, 4 times higher exposure and 3 times higher Cmax were observed on day 15 when compared with the first dose.

Over the dose range from 50 to 400 mg, on day 1 and day 15 of cycle 1, exposure (AUC and Cmax) seemed to increase in a dose-proportional manner. At 800 mg, the exposure seemed to increase more than proportionally compared with the lower doses. The interpatient variability of exposures was moderate to high (Supplementary Table S4).

BI 1701963 was excreted in urine with a geometric mean cumulative fraction of the dose over 24 hours (fe0–24,ss) between 0.176% and 5.13%. Geometric means of fe0–24,ss increased from day 1 to day 15, with larger increases of fe0–24,ss values for 600 and 800 mg dose levels. The plasma clearance estimated after oral administration was moderate, dose-dependent, and in the range of 20.5 to 123 mL/minute after the first dose.
The apparent terminal elimination half-life ranged from 10 to 14 hours at 50 to 400 mg (study NCT04111458) and > 20 hours at > 400 mg (all studies).

The average exposure of BI 1701963 was higher in the Asian studies (NCT04835714 and NCT04627142) in comparison with NCT04111458. In the Asian studies, around 3.5- to 4.5-fold higher exposure (AUC0–tz,ss) was observed at 400 mg compared with NCT04111458. At 600 mg, around a twofold higher exposure was seen in Japanese and Chinese patients, and at 800 mg, a 2.5-fold higher exposure was observed in Chinese patients. Due to low patient numbers with ILD, it was not possible to draw firm conclusions on the relationship between dose/exposure and the risk of developing this AE. Based on data collected following the first dose, it was observed that the two patients from NCT04627142 had very high steady state exposure, whereas the patient treated in NCT04835714 had comparatively low exposure.
In NCT04111458, AUC and Cmax of BI 1701963 were similar after coadministration of trametinib; the exposure of trametinib was not influenced by the coadministration of BI 1701963.

sec.title: Pharmacodynamics
sec.p: In NCT04111458, minor biomarker modulation with BI 1701963 as monotherapy or in combination with trametinib was observed, as indicated by generally minor decreases in H-scores for Ki-67 and pERK from screening to day 16 of treatment across most doses, representing small changes in the proliferative index and downstream signaling (Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: KRAS mutations are implicated in one in seven of all human cancers, including pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, and NSCLC (1). Here, we present data from three phase I studies investigating the SOS1 inhibitor BI 1701963 as monotherapy or in combination with trametinib in patients with KRAS mutation-positive solid tumors.

The MTD of BI 1701963 monotherapy was defined as 800 mg, based on two DLT observed in two of nine patients (22.2%) treated at this dose in NCT04111458. DLT were reported in two patients each in NCT04835714 (both at 600 mg) and NCT04627142 (both at 800 mg) during the MTD evaluation period. Overall, one patient (1.8%) experienced a confirmed partial response, and 12 patients (21.8%) had confirmed stable disease.

In NCT04835714 and NCT04627142, three Asian patients with colorectal cancer experienced fatal ILD during the first treatment cycle at dose levels of 600 mg (n = 1) and 800 mg (n = 2), defined as drug-related by the investigator. Despite the risk factors for ILD in these patients, including lung metastases, a history of smoking, and pulmonary artery thrombosis, it could not be excluded that BI 1701963 caused or contributed to these events.

On average, a 2.5-fold higher exposure was measured in Asian patients relative to Western patients; however, currently available data do not allow a conclusion on whether there was a relationship between dose or exposure and observed ILD. The two patients from NCT04627142 had very high exposure in steady state, whereas the patient in study NCT04835714 had comparatively low exposure based on data for the first dose, and exposure was not measured again following repetitive dosing. Two KRAS-targeted therapies, adagrasib and sotorasib, are associated with increased cases of pneumonitis and drug-induced ILD (21–24), respectively, suggesting that the occurrence of ILD may be a class effect AE of KRAS inhibitors. In addition, ILD has also been reported for some drugs acting on other components of the RAS pathway, including MEK inhibitors (such as trametinib), BRAF inhibitors (such as vemurafenib), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitors (such as trastuzumab deruxtecan), and EGFR inhibitors (such as osimertinib; refs. 25–28). No lung-related or hematologic side effects were observed in BI 1701963 preclinical toxicology studies. As a result of these analyses combined with high treatment discontinuation rates, it was not possible to draw firm conclusions on the efficacy of BI 1701963 given as monotherapy or in combination with trametinib; therefore, Boehringer Ingelheim decided to discontinue the NCT04835714 and NCT04627142 trials and further clinical development of BI 1701963. It will, however, be interesting to observe the pulmonary safety profile of other SOS1 inhibitors that are in development.

In these early-phase trials, the pharmacokinetic characteristics of BI 1701963 monotherapy were broadly consistent with expectations based on preclinical data. However, limited efficacy was observed, with only one patient in the monotherapy trial achieving a partial response. No correlations were seen between increased exposure or the presence of KRAS mutations and BI 1701963 antitumor activity. Pharmacodynamic data from the first-in-human study (Ki-67 and pERK) suggested little target engagement in tumor tissue, consistent with the overall lack of antitumor efficacy. Ki-67 is not uniformly expressed in solid tumors (29, 30), and patients in the biomarker study were not selected for the presence of Ki-67; therefore, it is possible that low baseline expression impaired the detection of positive signals associated with treatment. pERK data were inconclusive, most likely due to signal decay during biopsy retrieval (31).

In a large dose-escalation trial for trametinib (n = 206), the most common treatment-related AE were rash or dermatitis acneiform (n = 165, 80%) and diarrhea (n = 87, 42%), most of which were grade 1 or 2 (32). The AE profile of BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib was consistent with MAPK pathway inhibition (rash, liver enzyme elevations, and hypertension; ref. 33), indicating a possible synergistic effect arising from targeting MEK and SOS1 simultaneously; however, this did not result in clinical responses. In NCT04111458, data from the combination of BI 1701963 with trametinib indicated that the highest explored combination dose (200 mg/1 mg) was below the predicted therapeutically active dose. Although four patients (33%) experienced stable disease, no OR were observed.

The high number of patients experiencing AE and discontinuing treatment was unexpected for the combination arm based on preclinical data; this observation led to the decision to prematurely discontinue the clinical development of BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib. This study is ongoing, with one patient still on treatment after 319 days at data cutoff (BI 1701963 in combination with trametinib; 50 mg/0.5 mg). Despite the findings, these data will inform future research into therapies for patients with KRAS mutation-positive cancers (34).

Several functional classes of KRAS inhibitors are currently under clinical development. Beyond KRASG12C inhibitors (12–14), investigational agents that target KRASG12D include the KRASG12D inhibitor zoldonrasib (RMC-9805) and the KRASG12D degrader ASP3082 (35, 36). Additional classes of therapeutics in development include pan-KRAS inhibitors [e.g., BI 3706674 (37), under investigation in the phase I NCT06056024 study], and pan-RAS inhibitors [e.g., RMC-6236 (38, 39)]. Early signs of efficacy and tolerability have been reported in phase I clinical trials for KRASG12D inhibitors and pan-RAS inhibitors (39, 40). However, to date, there is still no approved targeted therapy for patients with KRAS mutation-positive tumors, other than those with KRASG12C.

Based on learnings from KRASG12C inhibitors, it is necessary to consider combinations with inhibitors of EGFR, SOS1, or SHP2 to enhance the durability of the response (41, 42). Several SOS1 inhibitors are currently under investigation, including MRTX0902 in patients with solid tumors harboring mutations in the KRAS–MAPK pathway (NCT05578092; refs. 42, 43), BAY3498264 in patients with KRASG12C in combination with sotorasib (NCT06659341; ref. 34), KQB198 in patients with hematologic malignancies alone and in combination with dasatinib (NCT06645886) and in patients with solid tumors alone and in combination with osimertinib (NCT06507306), and ZG2001 in patients with KRAS-mutated solid tumors (NCT06237413). The development of a novel SOS1 inhibitor with an improved profile may lead to fewer AE and might help enhance the durability of response to KRAS/RAS inhibitors in combination, addressing the unmet need for effective treatment to target a broad range of KRAS-mutant cancers.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: To ensure independent interpretation of clinical study results and enable authors to fulfill their roles and obligations under the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) criteria, Boehringer Ingelheim grants all external authors access to relevant clinical study data. In adherence to the Boehringer Ingelheim Policy on Transparency and Publication of Clinical Study Data, scientific and medical researchers can request access to clinical study data, typically 1 year after approval has been granted by major regulatory authorities or after the termination of the development program. Researchers should use the https://vivli.org/ link to request access to study data and visit https://www.clinicalstudies.boehringer-ingelheim.com/msw/datatransparency for further information.
